body: Shungite is a black rock with a high carbon content. The commercial stone is quarried in Karelia, in north west Russia, and takes its name from the village of Shunga. That is a fact about the mineral, not about this piece: the listing does not say where this one came from.
Elite Noble is a trade word for the shiny, high carbon sort. No assay comes with it, so this page prints no carbon figure of its own.
One. The name is plural and the listing says one piece of about 10 g, so one is what this page promises.
If a second turns up in the envelope, that is the shop being generous rather than the listing being kept.

acc.summary: What this page does not say
body: The listing this piece came from makes a number of statements about what it does and where to put it, several of them about water. None of them are repeated here, and none of them are made here in different words either.
Water Stones is the name printed on the listing. On this page it is a name and nothing else.
Sent out from 599 Smithdown Road, Liverpool, Tuesday to Sunday. UK delivery is free over £50, or you can collect from the shop between 10 and 6, any day except Monday.

spec.label: Objects · 03
spec.intro: A weight, a count and a price. The rest of the sheet is what the listing does not print, including any reason why this piece costs what it does against the heavier one.
spec.caption: Shungite Water Stones
rows: Shungite, a black rock with a high carbon content. One piece, nothing added.
One piece, as printed, in spite of the plural in the name.
£29.99 for one piece. The Elite Noble Shungite Stone on the same shelf is 20 to 30 g and costs £26.99. Neither listing explains the difference, so neither does this page.
The listing calls it Elite Noble, the trade word for the shiny, high carbon sort. No assay comes with it, so no carbon percentage appears here.
Not printed. The listing calls the size compact and gives no measurements.
Not printed. The listing does not say whether the piece is raw, tumbled or polished.
Not printed for this piece. Shungite as a mineral is quarried in Karelia, north west Russia.
None supplied. No assay, no laboratory report, no purity certificate.
Water Stones is the product name. What the listing says about water is not repeated on this page and is not implied on it either.
The listing prints a suggested use. It cannot be separated from claims we are not able to make, so none of it is carried across.
The listing carries the sentence that the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease. It is an American sentence and it does not make the paragraphs above it lawful here.
Anybody. It is an object, not something you take.
It is not a food and it is not a supplement. Do not put it in your mouth, and keep it away from young children, who put small hard things in theirs.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: There are three figures on this sheet that the listing gives us: one piece, about 10 g, £29.99. Everything else the listing says is about what the piece is meant to do, and that is the part a shop page in Britain is not allowed to print. So it is not here, and the gaps are named instead.

reiss.label: From Reiss
paras: Ten grams for £29.99, against twenty to thirty grams for £26.99 on the same shelf. Those are the two figures as they are listed. I am not going to explain the gap between them, because the listing does not explain it to me either, and a shop page inventing a reason is how the whole trade got into this state.

The rest of what that listing says about this piece is about water. None of it is on this page. The name stays because it is the name on the box, and a name is the one place a word like that is allowed to sit without being proved.
reiss.pull: Ten grams for twenty nine ninety nine. Those are the figures as listed.
